Toyota's enterprise IAM manages corporate user accounts. The system manages accounts for PLCs, SCADA, HMI operators, and engineering workstations using the OT roles: operator, maintenance, and engineering.

control_name: Account Management | Automated System Account Management
implementation_description: Provisioning and deprovisioning of operator and maintenance accounts on OT devices and HMIs is automated through the enterprise IAM.

control_name: Account Management | Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management
implementation_description: The enterprise IAM creates temporary and emergency accounts for OT maintenance and vendor access as time-limited accounts that expire automatically.
Inactive OT device and HMI accounts are disabled automatically after an organization-defined period. Enterprise IAM disables corporate users; system-level configuration disables OT-specific accounts.
Account creation, modification, and deletion events on OT devices and HMIs are logged and forwarded to Toyota's enterprise SIEM.

Operator sessions on OT devices, HMIs, and engineering workstations end automatically after an organization-defined period of inactivity. This matches the plant practice of automatic log-off where the function is available (TMMK, 2023, p. 14).

control_name: Account Management | Disable Accounts for High-risk Individuals
implementation_description: Toyota disables accounts for individuals flagged as high-risk through its enterprise HR and security processes, and propagates the action to OT devices and HMIs through the enterprise IAM.
Enterprise IAM enforces approved authorizations for user authentication, and OT device-level access controls enforce system-level operations on OT devices, HMIs, and SCADA systems.

OT DMZ firewalls with allowlist ACLs, VLAN segmentation, and network isolation control flows between corporate and OT networks. Only explicitly defined traffic crosses segments, including each Purdue transition (Enterprise IT, OT DMZ, Ops VLAN, Control VLAN, Floor VLAN) (TMMK, 2023, pp. 4–5).

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Object Security and Privacy Attributes
implementation_description: VLAN tags, firewall rules, and IP/subnet identifiers serve as the security attributes the OT DMZ firewalls use to apply allowlist ACLs.
OT processes run in separate processing domains (production control, engineering, maintenance), each in its own network segment with defined flow policies.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Flow Control of Encrypted Information
implementation_description: TLS inspection and IPsec enforcement at the OT DMZ firewalls keep encrypted traffic between corporate and OT networks within the flow policy.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | One-way Flow Mechanisms
implementation_description: One-way flows are used where only one-way transfer is needed, such as OT-to-corporate monitoring feeds and read-only inventory data shared with the AGV and DCS (TMMK, 2023, p. 4).

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Security and Privacy Policy Filters
implementation_description: OT DMZ firewall rulesets act as policy filters that apply Toyota's enterprise security policy and OT-specific requirements to every flow.
Changes to firewall rules and ACLs are reviewed and approved by authorized OT network administrators before deployment.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Enable and Disable Security or Privacy Policy Filters
implementation_description: Security policy filters can be enabled or disabled only through the OT DMZ firewall management interfaces, under change management, by authorized OT network administrators.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Configuration of Security or Privacy Policy Filters
implementation_description: Filter configurations are set through OT DMZ firewall rule sets and ACLs, managed through change management, and documented in this SSP.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Detection of Unsanctioned Information
implementation_description: OT network monitoring and intrusion detection identify traffic that violates the defined flow policies. IDS/IPS sit at the edge DMZ with remote probes watching the OT DMZ and lower networks (TMMK, 2023, p. 13).
OT DMZ firewalls authenticate network domains through mutual TLS and IPsec tunnel authentication before allowing inter-domain traffic.
Firewalls and network security tools used for flow enforcement come from Toyota's approved vendor list and meet enterprise security standards.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Physical or Logical Separation of Information Flows
implementation_description: Flows are separated logically through VLANs, subnets, and dedicated firewall interfaces and zones, and physically where networks are separate, such as the air-gapped R&D network (TMMK, 2023, p. 9).
Flows are separated logically through VLANs, subnets, and dedicated firewall interfaces and zones, and physically where networks are separate, such as the air-gapped R&D network (TMMK, 2023, p. 9).

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Audit Filtering Actions
implementation_description: Firewall rule evaluations, ACL matches, and denied-traffic events are logged and forwarded to Toyota's enterprise SIEM.

control_name: Information Flow Enforcement | Process Requirements for Information Transfer
implementation_description: Firewall ACLs enforce process requirements for transfers between corporate and OT networks, and change management governs any changes to those transfer rules.

Enterprise IAM defines role-based access, and the OT-specific roles (operator, maintenance, engineering) are enforced at the system level so no single role can operate, maintain, and administer the same asset.
Users receive only the access they need for assigned tasks. Enterprise IAM enforces RBAC for corporate users, and OT device-level permissions are configured at the system level.

control_name: Least Privilege | Authorize Access to Security Functions
implementation_description: Access to security functions (firewall administration, PLC programming, HMI configuration) is limited to authorized OT engineers and administrators through enterprise IAM and system-level access controls.

control_name: Least Privilege | Non-privileged Access for Nonsecurity Functions
implementation_description: Users with access to security functions use non-privileged accounts or roles for non-security work. TMMK: engineers and administrators use standard accounts for email and office work; privileged OT accounts are used only for PLC, DCS, and firewall changes.

Restrict privileged accounts on the system to set personnel or roles. TMMK: PLC programming, DCS configuration, and OT firewall administration are limited to named OT engineers; enterprise IT admin rights do not carry into OT.

control_name: Least Privilege | Review of User Privileges
implementation_description: Review assigned privileges on a set schedule and reassign or remove any no longer needed. TMMK: the enterprise access review covers OT accounts, including local PLC/HMI accounts and vendor accounts.

control_name: Least Privilege | Log Use of Privileged Functions
implementation_description: Log the execution of privileged functions. TMMK: log PLC program downloads, setpoint and safety-limit overrides, and firewall rule changes.

control_name: Least Privilege | Prohibit Non-privileged Users from Executing Privileged Functions
implementation_description: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions. TMMK: operator HMI roles can view and operate; changing PLC logic or safety limits needs an engineering role (read vs. write privilege tiers).

Limit consecutive invalid logon attempts and lock the account or delay further attempts when the limit is exceeded. TMMK: enforced through enterprise IAM on engineering workstations, admin accounts, and servers.
Display an approved system use notification before granting access. TMMK: enterprise banner on workstations and servers.

Lock the device after a set period of inactivity or on user request, and keep it locked until the user re-authenticates. TMMK: auto log-off is already used at computers, monitoring stations, and HMIs where available (TMMK, 2023, p. 14). Operator HMIs that must stay visible, or be usable at once in an emergency, are exempt and protected by physical access control instead (SP 800-82r3).
The device lock conceals what was on the display with a publicly viewable image. TMMK: applies to engineering workstations and supervisor stations.

Automatically end a user session after set conditions or trigger events. TMMK: applies to remote and engineering sessions into the OT DMZ and control networks; local operator sessions follow the AC-11 exemption.

control_name: Permitted Actions Without Identification or Authentication
implementation_description: Identify and document the user actions allowed without identification or authentication, with rationale. TMMK: limited to emergency actions at HMIs, such as e-stop and viewing alarm status, so operators are never blocked in an emergency.

Set usage restrictions, connection requirements, and guidance for each type of remote access, and authorize each type before use. TMMK: enterprise remote access policy applies; remote access into the OT networks, including vendor support, is authorized per connection and passes through the OT DMZ (crossing X1).
Monitor and control remote access methods with automated mechanisms. TMMK: remote sessions into the OT networks are logged and monitored centrally.

control_name: Remote Access | Protection of Confidentiality and Integrity Using Encryption
implementation_description: Protect the confidentiality and integrity of remote access sessions with cryptography. TMMK: enterprise VPN terminating in the OT DMZ; OT devices that can't encrypt are reached only through it.

control_name: Remote Access | Managed Access Control Points
implementation_description: Route all remote access through authorized, managed network access control points. TMMK: one managed entry point in the OT DMZ; no direct remote connections to the Ops, Control, or Floor VLANs (crossings X1, X2).

control_name: Remote Access | Privileged Commands and Access
implementation_description: Allow privileged commands and security-relevant access over remote access only for set needs, and document the rationale in the security plan. TMMK: remote PLC programming or firewall changes only for documented vendor or emergency support, logged under AC-6(9).

control_name: Remote Access | Disconnect or Disable Access
implementation_description: Provide the capability to disconnect or disable remote access within a set time. TMMK: OT staff can cut remote sessions at the OT DMZ entry point without disrupting line operations, and are trained to do it.
Authenticate set remote commands with set mechanisms. TMMK: remote commands that change PLC logic, setpoints, or AGV routing are authenticated before they execute (R-03).

Set configuration and connection requirements for each type of wireless access, and authorize each type before use. TMMK: the AGV and Environmental SCADA systems use unpublished, encrypted SSIDs preprogrammed onto designated devices (TMMK, 2023, pp. 4, 6-7); software installs use an encrypted wireless VLAN (p. 5); no wireless is allowed in the R&D area (p. 9).

The TMMK will protect wireless access to organizational systems by authenticating authorized users and/or devices and implementing approved encryption mechanisms. Wireless-enabled manufacturing equipment, devices, sensors, and other systems will use organization-approved authentication and encryption configurations to protect wireless communications from unauthorized access and disclosure (p. 4, 6, 7, 9). (R-01, R-03)

The TMMK will disable wireless networking capabilities, including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, on system components when they are not required for authorized operational functions. Wireless capabilities required for manufacturing or OT operations will remain enabled and will be protected in accordance with applicable wireless security requirements. (R-03)

The TMMK plant will establish configuration and connection requirements for organization-controlled mobile devices used within the manufacturing environment. The line's only mobile device, the operator and mechanic handheld, will connect only to the Ops VLAN (RAV4-PL-OPS) and will not reach the Control or Floor VLANs directly. Toyota's enterprise mobile device management will set enrollment and configuration requirements, and TMMK will enforce them on the line. (R-01, R-03)

control_name: Access Control for Mobile Devices | Full Device or Container-based Encryption
implementation_description: TMMK will use full-device encryption on the operator and mechanic handheld on the Ops VLAN (RAV4-PL-OPS) so that a lost or borrowed device does not expose OT data or credentials. (R-01, R-03)

The TMMK will establish and enforce requirements for the use of external systems that access the OT environment or process, store, or transmit organizational information. Access from external systems will be authorized based on defined security requirements and applicable connection or processing agreements. (R-03)

control_name: Use of External Systems | Limits on Authorized Use
implementation_description: The TMMK will permit authorized personnel to use external systems to access the OT environment only after verifying required security controls on the external system or establishing an approved system connection or processing agreement with the external system owner. (R-03)

control_name: Use of External Systems | Portable Storage Devices — Restricted Use
implementation_description: The TMMK will restrict the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices on external systems accessing or supporting the OT environment. Portable storage devices will be used only under organization-defined restrictions and approved conditions to reduce the risk of unauthorized access, malware introduction, and information disclosure. (R-02)

The TMMK will ensure that authorized personnel verify sharing partners have appropriate access authorizations before sharing restricted OT or organizational information. The plant will use approved procedures and, where applicable, automated mechanisms to support information-sharing and collaboration decisions. (R-03)

The TMMK will designate authorized personnel to publish information to publicly accessible systems. Authorized personnel will be trained to prevent disclosure of nonpublic information, and proposed content will be reviewed prior to publication. Publicly accessible content will be reviewed at an organization-defined frequency, and any nonpublic information identified will be removed. (R-05)

control_name: Separation of System and User Functionality
implementation_description: System-level functions (PLC logic, SCADA control) are separated from user-level functions (HMI operator screens). Engineering workstations keep system administration separate from operator functions. HMIs and supervisor workstations sit on networks separate from the PLCs (TMMK, 2023, p. 8).
VLAN segmentation and OT device access controls stop unintended information transfer through shared resources on PLCs, HMIs, and engineering workstations.

Corporate firewalls, OT DMZ firewalls, and network segmentation protect against denial-of-service, with rate limiting and VLAN isolation shielding OT devices and PLCs from resource exhaustion. A redundant fiber ring and active-active servers add availability (TMMK, 2023, p. 13).

Toyota's corporate firewalls (inherited) and OT DMZ firewalls with allowlist ACLs (system-specific) protect the boundary. Internal firewalls, VLANs, and the OT DMZ separate the ICS/OT network from the business network, and centrally managed firewalls sit at every network boundary (TMMK, 2023, p. 13).
All corporate-to-OT connections pass through designated OT DMZ firewall interfaces, which limits external access points. Only authorized OT network administrators manage them.

External connections, such as supplier EDI feeds and remote vendor maintenance, pass through Toyota's corporate network and the OT DMZ, where allowlist ACLs restrict traffic to explicitly defined sources and destinations.

control_name: Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception
implementation_description: OT DMZ firewalls deny all traffic between the corporate and ICS/OT networks unless an ACL explicitly allows it.

control_name: Boundary Protection | Split Tunneling for Remote Devices
implementation_description: Remote access, such as vendor maintenance, goes through Toyota's corporate VPN and the OT DMZ. Split tunneling is prevented so all remote traffic is inspected.

control_name: Boundary Protection | Route Traffic to Authenticated Proxy Servers
implementation_description: Traffic between corporate and OT networks goes through authenticated proxy servers in the OT DMZ, where it is inspected and authenticated before reaching ICS/OT devices.

TLS and IPsec protect communications between corporate networks and OT devices. Protocol traffic inside the OT network relies on network segmentation. Wireless links for the AGV and environmental SCADA use an unpublished, encrypted SSID reserved for the system (TMMK, 2023, pp. 6–7).

control_name: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection
implementation_description: TLS and IPsec protect traffic crossing the OT DMZ and the corporate-OT boundary. Software installs travel over an encrypted wireless VLAN to the TPM-equipped unit (TMMK, 2023, p. 9).
OT network switches and firewalls end connections at the end of a session or after an organization-defined period of inactivity.
Toyota's enterprise PKI provides key management for corporate-OT communications. OT-specific key management covers ICS device certificates and VPN tunnels.
FIPS-validated cryptographic modules protect communications and data. OT devices use cryptographic protection for authentication and transmission where the device platform supports it.
Collaborative devices on the line, such as HMI screens and video monitoring, are controlled to prevent unauthorized remote activation, and remote collaboration features are disabled when not in use.
Toyota's enterprise PKI and CA issue and manage certificates for corporate-OT communications, device authentication, and ICS device certificates.
Mobile code is restricted on the OT network. OT components run only approved mobile code in confined environments, under Toyota's enterprise mobile code policy.
Toyota's enterprise DNS answers queries from OT devices and provides data origin authentication for authoritative responses.

control_name: Secure Name/address Resolution Service (recursive or Caching Resolver)
implementation_description: OT devices use Toyota's enterprise recursive resolvers, which validate DNSSEC to confirm the origin and integrity of responses.

control_name: Architecture and Provisioning for Name/address Resolution Service
implementation_description: Toyota's enterprise DNS provides fault-tolerant, redundant name and address resolution for OT devices.
TLS and network segmentation protect session authenticity between OT devices, HMIs, and corporate systems.

Access controls and, where the device platform supports it, cryptographic mechanisms protect information at rest on PLCs, HMIs, and engineering workstations. Backups use write-once-read-many (WORM) storage (TMMK, 2023, p. 13).

control_name: Protection of Information at Rest | Cryptographic Protection
implementation_description: Full-disk or file-level encryption protects sensitive information on OT engineering workstations and HMIs where the platform supports it.

PLCs, HMIs, and engineering workstations keep separate execution domains for different processes to block unauthorized information flow between them. The hypervisor layer in the lightweight TPM design isolates processes in vehicle software delivery (TMMK, 2023, p. 9).

TMMK: Enterprise IT's centrally managed patching (remote DMZ server) covers servers and applications, deploying patches once tested and verified (TMMK, 2023, p. 13). PLC, HMI, and DCS firmware get vendor-validated patches installed in scheduled maintenance windows (RMF Task I-2).

control_name: Flaw Remediation | Automated Flaw Remediation Status
implementation_description: Use automated mechanisms to check, on a set schedule, whether components have the applicable security-relevant software and firmware updates installed. TMMK: the enterprise patch tool reports on servers and workstations; the OT asset inventory (CM-8) tracks firmware versions on PLCs, HMIs, and AGVs.

Detect and eradicate malicious code at system entry and exit points, keep protection updated, scan on a schedule and in real time, and define the response to detections. TMMK: enterprise endpoint protection runs on HMIs, engineering workstations, and OT DMZ servers; PLCs cannot host it. Add a malware scan to the existing wipe-and-verify step for the R&D transfer devices (TMMK, 2023, p. 13).

Monitor the system to detect attacks, indicators of attack, and unauthorized local, network, and remote connections; place monitoring at strategic points; protect and report monitoring data. TMMK: IDS/IPS at the Edge DMZ with remote probes into the OT DMZ and lower networks (TMMK, 2023, p. 13) reports to the enterprise SOC. The line adds OT-protocol monitoring at the Control and Floor VLAN boundaries (RMF Task M-2).

control_name: System Monitoring | Automated Tools and Mechanisms for Real-time Analysis
implementation_description: Employ automated tools and mechanisms to support near real-time analysis of events. TMMK: OT anomaly detection baselines normal Modbus and PROFINET traffic and flags deviations, such as unauthenticated writes to a PLC (R-03).

control_name: System Monitoring | Inbound and Outbound Communications Traffic
implementation_description: Set criteria for unusual or unauthorized inbound and outbound traffic and monitor for it on a set schedule. TMMK: applies at each boundary crossing (X1 Enterprise IT to OT DMZ, X2 OT DMZ to industrial network) and on the AGV and software-install wireless segments (X4, X5).
Alert set personnel when system-generated indicators of compromise occur. TMMK: OT sensor alerts go to the enterprise SOC and the line's OT security staff, and feed the IR-4 incident loop.

Receive security alerts, advisories, and directives from external sources, generate internal ones, disseminate them, and act on them within set time frames. TMMK: the enterprise receives general advisories; the line's OT team tracks CISA ICS advisories and vendor notices for its own PLC, SCADA, DCS, and AGV products (RMF Phase 6).

Employ integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to set software, firmware, and information, and take set actions when changes are found. TMMK: SafetySense 2.0 packages go into a version-controlled registry with an immutable changelog, the vehicle TPM verifies them before install, and Final QA checks and records hashes (TMMK, 2023, pp. 5, 10, 13). The RMF adds signing in the R&D enclave, and PLC logic is compared against its CM-2 baseline (R-02, R-03).

control_name: Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity | Integrity Checks
implementation_description: Perform integrity checks of set software, firmware, and information at startup, at set transitional states or security-relevant events, or on a set schedule.
